difficultyReason: Two-step causal chain (new medication → reduced inflammation → improved mobility). The weakener attacks the move from evidence to conclusion by offering an alternative explanation for the observed improvement. Distractors include a strengthener and an out-of-scope detail about the same medical domain.
stimulus: Researchers at a clinical trial administered a new anti-inflammatory drug to patients with rheumatoid arthritis over a twelve-week period. By the end of the trial, participants reported a 40 percent improvement in joint mobility. The researchers concluded that the drug's anti-inflammatory properties were responsible for the mobility gains.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All trial participants were also enrolled in a supervised physical therapy program that began at the same time as the drug regimen.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anti-inflammatory drugs have been shown in previous studies to reduce joint swelling in patients with rheumatoid arthritis.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some participants reported minor gastrointestinal side effects during the first two weeks of the trial.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The improvement in mobility was measured using a standardized assessment tool validated for arthritis research.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Patients who received a higher dose of the drug reported slightly greater mobility gains than those on the lower dose.

explanations.correct: If all participants were simultaneously enrolled in physical therapy, that program is a plausible alternative cause of the mobility improvements, undermining the researchers' causal attribution to the drug.
explanations.A: Correct. Introduces a confounding variable—physical therapy—that could fully explain the observed improvement without any contribution from the drug.
explanations.B: Opposite-answer trap. Prior evidence that anti-inflammatory drugs reduce swelling strengthens the researchers' conclusion rather than weakening it.
explanations.C: Out-of-scope. Side effects in some participants are irrelevant to whether the drug caused mobility improvements in the group as a whole.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant. Validating the measurement tool bolsters the reliability of the data; it does not challenge the causal claim.
explanations.E: Strengthener trap. A dose-response relationship is consistent with the drug being causally responsible for mobility gains.

difficultyReason: Predictive argument: economist predicts policy outcome from a single historical precedent. The weakener attacks the analogy by exposing a relevant disanalogy. Distractors include a same-topic strengthener and a too-narrow answer that questions data quality without touching the conclusion.
stimulus: An economist argues that eliminating the city's commercial rent-control ordinance will stimulate new business formation. She points to Hillcrest, a neighboring municipality that repealed its rent-control law five years ago and subsequently saw a 25 percent increase in new business registrations over the following three years.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the economist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The city currently has a higher commercial vacancy rate than Hillcrest had at the time of its repeal.

choices.label: B
choices.text: During the three years following Hillcrest's repeal, the regional economy as a whole experienced unusually rapid expansion that did not affect the city.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several economists have argued that rent control can reduce the overall quality of commercial real estate stock over time.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The city's rent-control ordinance was enacted more recently than Hillcrest's was.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Business registration data in Hillcrest may have included renewals as well as genuinely new enterprises.

explanations.correct: If Hillcrest's business surge coincided with a regional economic boom that did not affect the city, then the repeal of rent control may not have caused the increase—and replicating the policy change in the city cannot be expected to produce the same result. This is a disanalogy that severs the analogical basis of the prediction.
explanations.A: Accurate but irrelevant. A higher vacancy rate might even support the economist's view that loosening rent control could attract new tenants; it does not undermine the causal claim.
explanations.B: Correct. Reveals that Hillcrest's growth may have been driven by an external economic factor absent in the city, breaking the analogy.
explanations.C: Strengthener trap. Supporting the view that rent control harms commercial real estate reinforces the economist's case for repeal.
explanations.D: Too narrow. The relative age of the ordinances does not bear on whether repealing the city's ordinance would replicate Hillcrest's business growth.
explanations.E: Too narrow. Even if the data overcount new registrations, the argument's core analogy stands unless we know the overcounting is systematic enough to eliminate the apparent effect.

difficultyReason: Causal-predictive argument in environmental science. The weakener attacks the causal inference by offering an alternative explanation for the observed data. One distractor attacks a peripheral premise without touching the conclusion; another strengthens.
stimulus: Biologists studying a coastal wetland recorded a 30 percent decline in shorebird populations over a decade. During that same period, an industrial facility upstream discharged elevated levels of heavy metals into the watershed. The biologists concluded that heavy-metal contamination was responsible for the shorebird decline.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Heavy metals are known to accumulate in the small fish and invertebrates that shorebirds typically eat.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The industrial facility's discharge levels exceeded federal safety thresholds throughout the monitoring period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A highly contagious avian disease spread through shorebird populations along the entire coastline during the same decade, causing comparable declines in wetlands unaffected by industrial discharge.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The biologists used aerial surveys to count shorebird populations, a method that can undercount birds sheltering in dense vegetation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Heavy-metal contamination has been linked to reproductive failure in several other bird species studied in laboratory settings.

explanations.correct: If a contagious disease caused similar declines in unaffected wetlands, the heavy-metal contamination need not be the cause of this wetland's decline, providing a compelling alternative explanation.
explanations.A: Strengthener trap. Establishing a plausible biological mechanism for how heavy metals could harm shorebirds supports the causal conclusion.
explanations.B: Strengthener trap. Confirming that discharge levels were dangerously high bolsters the claim that contamination was the culprit.
explanations.C: Correct. Comparable declines in sites without industrial discharge indicate a region-wide alternative cause, undermining the specific causal attribution.
explanations.D: Too narrow. Undercounting due to methodology would affect the accuracy of the absolute numbers but does not explain why a decline occurred, leaving the causal claim intact.
explanations.E: Strengthener trap. Laboratory evidence linking heavy metals to bird reproductive failure supports the conclusion.

difficultyReason: Two-step policy argument: policy change caused behavioral shift, behavioral shift caused outcome. Weakener attacks the second causal link. Distractors include an opposite answer and a shift-in-subject trap.
stimulus: After a city council enacted a mandatory helmet law for cyclists, emergency room admissions for serious head injuries among cyclists dropped by 35 percent over two years. A public health official concluded that the helmet law was responsible for the reduction in serious head injuries.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Studies in other cities have found that mandatory helmet laws increase overall cyclist safety.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The helmet law was accompanied by a significant increase in cycling infrastructure, including protected lanes, which substantially reduced the number of cyclist-vehicle collisions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Compliance with the helmet law among cyclists under age 18 was higher than compliance among adult cyclists.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several neighboring cities without helmet laws also recorded decreases in cyclist head injuries during the same period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Emergency room physicians noted that the head injuries they did treat during the post-law period were less severe on average.

explanations.correct: If cities without helmet laws also experienced declines in cyclist head injuries over the same period, a region-wide factor—not the helmet law—may be responsible, undermining the official's causal claim.
explanations.A: Strengthener trap. Evidence from other cities supporting helmet law effectiveness reinforces the official's conclusion.
explanations.B: Alternative explanation that could weaken, but it does not undermine the helmet law's causal role as clearly as D; moreover, improved infrastructure might explain some but not all of the reduction. However, D provides a cleaner, direct challenge by showing the effect occurred without the cause.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant. Differential compliance rates by age do not address whether the law as a whole caused the injury reduction.
explanations.D: Correct. Parallel declines in cities without the law suggest a common regional factor, not the helmet law, is the real cause.
explanations.E: Accurate but irrelevant. The severity of remaining injuries does not undermine the claim that the law reduced the number of serious injuries.

difficultyReason: Causal argument in technology. The weakener introduces a confounder that explains the correlation. Distractors include a too-narrow methodological objection and a strengthener using the same domain.
stimulus: A technology firm introduced an AI-assisted code-review tool for its software engineers in January. By June of the same year, the number of software defects reaching production had fallen by 45 percent compared to the prior six-month period. The firm's engineering director concluded that the AI tool was responsible for the dramatic improvement in software quality.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most calls into question the engineering director's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The AI tool flagged an average of twelve potential defects per code review session during the six-month period.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In January, the firm also replaced its most error-prone legacy codebase with a newly architected system that had been under development for two years.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Software engineers at the firm reported high satisfaction with the AI tool's interface and recommendations.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The defect-tracking system used by the firm counts only defects reported by end users, potentially undercounting internal testing failures.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Other technology firms that adopted similar AI code-review tools also reported reductions in production defects.

explanations.correct: Replacing the error-prone legacy codebase at the same time as the AI tool's introduction provides an alternative explanation for the defect reduction, undermining the director's attribution of the improvement to the AI tool alone.
explanations.A: Strengthener trap. Showing the AI tool actively caught defects supports the causal claim.
explanations.B: Correct. A simultaneous and highly consequential infrastructure change is a confounding variable that could fully account for the drop in production defects.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant. Engineer satisfaction with the tool's interface does not establish that the tool caused fewer defects to reach production.
explanations.D: Too narrow. An undercounting issue would mean the true defect numbers are uncertain, but it does not explain why a decline occurred or attribute it to another cause.
explanations.E: Strengthener trap. Corroborating evidence from other firms supports the hypothesis that AI tools reduce defects.

difficultyReason: Analogical argument in law. The weakener exposes a disanalogy that severs the comparison. One distractor strengthens; another is a shift-in-subject trap.
stimulus: A defense attorney argued that her client should not be held liable for defamation because a court in a neighboring jurisdiction ruled in favor of a defendant who made nearly identical statements about a public official. Since the facts of the two cases are substantially similar, the attorney contended, the outcome should be the same.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the attorney's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The plaintiff in the current case is a private individual, not a public official, and private individuals bear a lower burden of proof in defamation claims than public officials do.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The neighboring jurisdiction's court cited the defendant's lack of malicious intent as a key factor in its ruling.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Defamation law varies somewhat from jurisdiction to jurisdiction due to differences in state statutes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The statements at issue in the neighboring jurisdiction's case were made in a published newspaper article, as in the current case.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The attorney's client has no prior history of defamatory statements.

explanations.correct: The attorney's argument rests on factual similarity between the cases. If the plaintiff's status differs in a legally decisive way—private individuals have a lower burden of proof—then the cases are not truly analogous, directly undermining the analogical reasoning.
explanations.A: Correct. Identifies a material legal disanalogy (public official vs. private individual) that invalidates the comparison and weakens the attorney's conclusion.
explanations.B: Too narrow. This explains why the other defendant won, but without knowing whether the current defendant also lacked malicious intent, it does not clearly weaken the attorney's argument—it could even provide a road map for the defense.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant. General jurisdictional variation is too vague to undermine this specific analogy unless the relevant statute in the current jurisdiction is shown to differ materially.
explanations.D: Strengthener trap. Confirming a factual similarity between the cases bolsters the analogy the attorney is drawing.
explanations.E: Shift-in-subject trap. The defendant's prior conduct is not relevant to whether the two cases are legally analogous.

difficultyReason: Causal generalization from sample in linguistics. Weakener attacks the representativeness of the sample. Distractors include a strengthener and an out-of-scope distractor.
stimulus: A linguist studied fifty bilingual children between the ages of four and six and found that those who regularly switched between their two languages during play—a behavior called code-switching—scored higher on executive function tests than those who did not code-switch. The linguist concluded that code-switching enhances executive function in bilingual children.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Children with stronger executive function are more likely to have the cognitive flexibility needed to code-switch in the first place.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Executive function tests for young children have been validated across multiple cultural and linguistic groups.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some monolingual children score as highly on executive function tests as the highest-scoring bilingual children in the study.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The bilingual children in the study spoke a variety of language pairs, including Spanish-English and Mandarin-English combinations.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Other studies have found that bilingualism in general, regardless of code-switching behavior, is associated with enhanced executive function.

explanations.correct: If children with stronger executive function are already more predisposed to code-switch, the causal direction may be reversed: executive function drives code-switching, not the other way around. This reversed-causation argument directly undermines the linguist's causal conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. Raises the possibility of reversed causation, which would explain the correlation without requiring that code-switching causes improved executive function.
explanations.B: Accurate but irrelevant. Validation of the test instrument does not bear on whether the causal relationship runs in the direction the linguist claims.
explanations.C: Out-of-scope. Monolingual children's scores are outside the scope of an argument about bilingual children who code-switch versus those who do not.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant. Language-pair diversity in the sample may strengthen the generalizability of the findings, not weaken the argument.
explanations.E: Too narrow. If general bilingualism already boosts executive function, the linguist's claim about code-switching specifically could still hold as an additional factor; this does not clearly weaken the conclusion.

difficultyReason: Predictive argument in ethics/policy about corporate disclosure. Weakener attacks the prediction by showing a disanalogy between predicted and actual conditions. One distractor is an unwarranted comparison; another strengthens.
stimulus: A consumer advocacy group argued that requiring corporations to publicly disclose the salaries of all employees will reduce income inequality within those firms. The group cited evidence that when a financial services company voluntarily published its full salary data two years ago, its internal pay gap between the highest- and lowest-paid employees narrowed by 18 percent within twelve months.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the argument's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The financial services company that voluntarily disclosed its salaries did so specifically because its leadership was already committed to reducing pay inequality, a motivation that mandatory disclosure would not instill in resistant firms.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mandatory pay-disclosure laws have been enacted in several European countries over the past decade.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Income inequality in financial services firms tends to be higher than in other industries due to the prevalence of performance bonuses.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Shareholders of publicly traded companies already have access to executive compensation data through annual reports.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Employees who learn that peers in comparable roles are paid more tend to negotiate more aggressively for raises.

explanations.correct: The advocacy group's argument depends on an analogy to a voluntary-disclosure case. If voluntary disclosure worked because leadership was already motivated to reduce inequality—a condition absent in firms that resist mandatory disclosure—the analogy breaks down, and the predicted effect of mandatory disclosure is undermined.
explanations.A: Correct. Exposes a critical disanalogy: the motivational context that made voluntary disclosure effective would be absent in companies compelled by law, severing the analogical basis for the prediction.
explanations.B: Accurate but irrelevant. The existence of such laws elsewhere says nothing about whether they achieved the goal of reducing income inequality.
explanations.C: Unwarranted comparison trap. Even if financial services firms have higher baseline inequality, this does not undermine the claim that disclosure reduces whatever level of inequality exists.
explanations.D: Too narrow. Executive compensation visibility is narrower than full salary disclosure; this does not address whether mandatory full disclosure would reduce inequality.
explanations.E: Strengthener trap. If disclosure prompts employees to negotiate higher wages, that mechanism supports the prediction that disclosure will narrow the pay gap.

difficultyReason: Causal argument in history. Weakener introduces a confounding variable. Distractors include a premise-attacking choice that doesn't touch the conclusion and a strengthener.
stimulus: Historians have noted that the Roman city of Pompeii had an unusually dense concentration of thermopolia—fast-food establishments—compared to other Roman cities of similar size. One historian argued that this high density of thermopolia indicates that Pompeii's residents had lower rates of home cooking than Romans in comparable cities, suggesting that Pompeii had a distinctive street-food culture driven by consumer preference for prepared meals.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Archaeological evidence indicates that a significant portion of Pompeii's population lived in multi-family apartment buildings that lacked kitchen facilities.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The thermopolia found in Pompeii offered a wider variety of foods than those excavated in other Roman cities.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Roman cookbooks from the same era suggest that home cooking was common among wealthy households throughout the empire.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some thermopolia in Pompeii were located adjacent to large private homes, suggesting their owners were affluent.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Historians have used thermopolia density as a proxy for urbanization levels in other ancient Mediterranean cities.

explanations.correct: If many residents lacked kitchen facilities due to apartment living, the high density of thermopolia would be explained by structural necessity rather than consumer preference for street food, undermining the historian's conclusion about a distinctive preference-driven culture.
explanations.A: Correct. Provides an alternative structural explanation—absence of home kitchens—that accounts for high thermopolia density without invoking a special cultural preference.
explanations.B: Accurate but irrelevant. Variety in menu offerings does not address whether the density of thermopolia reflects consumer preference versus structural necessity.
explanations.C: Too narrow. Evidence about wealthy households cooking at home does not clearly undermine the claim about Pompeii's population broadly, and does not address the structural explanation for density.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant. The wealth of thermopolia owners does not speak to why residents used them or whether preference or necessity drove demand.
explanations.E: Shift-in-subject trap. How other historians use thermopolia data in other contexts is irrelevant to whether this historian's specific causal inference about Pompeii is valid.

difficultyReason: Predictive causal argument in arts/cultural policy. Weakener attacks by showing the evidence does not generalize. Distractors include an opposite answer and a too-narrow premise-attacker.
stimulus: A municipal arts council proposed eliminating fees for gallery exhibitions in public museums, arguing that doing so would significantly increase attendance among lower-income residents. The council pointed to a pilot program at one city museum in which free admission on Sunday afternoons resulted in a 60 percent increase in visitors from lower-income zip codes during those hours.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Sunday afternoon free-admission program was heavily advertised through community outreach in lower-income neighborhoods, a marketing effort the council has no plans to replicate for the proposed fee elimination.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lower-income residents cited transportation costs, not admission fees, as the primary barrier to museum attendance in a survey conducted before the pilot program.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The museum that ran the pilot program is located closer to lower-income neighborhoods than most of the city's other public museums.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Eliminating fees would reduce museum revenues, potentially forcing cuts to educational programming.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several major cities that have adopted permanent free-admission policies report sustained increases in overall museum attendance.

explanations.correct: If lower-income residents themselves identify transportation—not admission fees—as the main barrier, then eliminating fees would not address the actual obstacle, making it unlikely that attendance among lower-income residents would significantly increase as predicted.
explanations.A: Weakens somewhat, but focuses on marketing as an omitted factor rather than directly undercutting the mechanism. B is stronger because it attacks the core causal assumption—that fees are the relevant barrier—whereas A only explains why the effect might be smaller in practice.
explanations.B: Correct. Directly challenges the load-bearing causal premise that admission fees are the primary barrier for lower-income residents, undermining the prediction that eliminating fees will significantly boost their attendance.
explanations.C: Too narrow. The pilot museum's location might explain why its results could be hard to replicate across all museums, but it does not undermine the core causal claim that free admission drives lower-income attendance.
explanations.D: Shift-in-subject trap. Potential budgetary consequences are a separate policy consideration; they do not weaken the prediction that attendance would increase.
explanations.E: Opposite-answer trap. Evidence from other cities sustaining increased attendance under free-admission policies strengthens the council's prediction.
